k3-fm-L07-P04.why:
The shell radius is the distance from x to the axis: x − (−1) = x + 1.
V = 2π∫₁³ (x+1)(1/x) dx = 2π∫₁³ (1 + 1/x) dx = 2π[x + ln x]₁³
= 2π(3 + ln3 − 1) = 2π(2 + ln 3) ≈ 19.47
Shifting the axis changes only the radius factor, never the height.

k3-fm-L09-P03.q: A force of 20 N stretches a spring 0.5 m beyond its natural length (so k = 40 N/m). Find the work to stretch it from 0.5 m to 1.2 m beyond natural length.
k3-fm-L09-P03.why:
W = ∫_{0.5}^{1.2} 40x dx = [20x²]_{0.5}^{1.2} = 20(1.44 − 0.25) = 23.8 J
The work formula ½k(b² − a²) gives the same thing: 20(1.44 − 0.25). Note the work is not proportional to distance; stretching farther costs progressively more.

k3-fm-L09-P05.q: A 40 ft chain weighing 3 lb/ft hangs from a winch, with a 60 lb weight attached at the bottom. Find the total work to wind it all up.
k3-fm-L09-P05.why:
The chain: with y the distance below the winch, a slice weighs 3 dy and rises y, so W = ∫₀⁴⁰ 3y dy = [3y²/2]₀⁴⁰ = 2400 ft·lb.
The weight is a single object lifted the full 40 ft: 60(40) = 2400 ft·lb.
Total: 4800 ft·lb
Point masses are multiplication, distributed masses are integration. Add the two contributions.

k91-fm-L10-P02.q: A cylindrical tank of radius 2 m and height 6 m holds water to a depth of 4 m. Find the work needed to pump all of the water out over the top. (Water: 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s².)
k91-fm-L10-P02.why:
Put y = 0 at the bottom. Each slice has area π(2)² = 4π and is lifted 6 − y to the top, so its weight per unit height is 1000(9.8)(4π) = 39200π. The water only fills 0 ≤ y ≤ 4, so the upper limit is 4, not 6.
W = ∫₀⁴ 39200π(6 − y) dy = 39200π[6y − y²/2]₀⁴ = 39200π(16) ≈ 1.97 × 10⁶ J
Integrate over the water, not over the tank. This is the most commonly missed detail in the section.

k91-fm-L10-P04.why:
Put y = 0 at the center of the sphere, so y runs from −3 to 3.
Radius of the slice: √(9 − y²), so A(y) = π(9 − y²).
Distance lifted to the top of the tank: 3 − y.
W = ∫₋₃³ 9800π(9 − y²)(3 − y) dy
Centering the coordinate at the sphere's center makes the radius formula clean. Putting y = 0 at the bottom works too but produces (y−3)² inside.

k91-fm-L10-P06.why:
Let d measure depth below the surface, 0 to 10.
F = ∫₀¹⁰ 1000(9.8)(d)(20) dd = 196000[d²/2]₀¹⁰ = 196000(50) = 9.8 × 10⁶ N
Check: this is the pressure at the plate's centroid (depth 5 m) times its area, 9800(5)(200) = 9.8 × 10⁶ N. That shortcut holds for any flat plate, not just rectangles, because pressure grows linearly with depth; for a rectangle the centroid is simply at mid-depth.

$hintKeys: ½sec x tan x + ½ln|sec x + tan x| + C

k5-fm-L16-P07.why:
Partial fractions: 1/(x² − 1) = ½[1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1)], so the antiderivative is ½ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| + C.
[(1/2)ln((x−1)/(x+1))]₂³ = ½[ln(2/4) − ln(1/3)] = ½[ln(1/2) + ln3] = ½ln(3/2) ≈ 0.203
Positive, as it should be: on [2,3] the integrand 1/(x²−1) is positive. Getting a negative value here would signal a sign error in the decomposition.

k5-fm-L17-P06.q: For each integral, name the first technique you would use, without solving: (a) ∫x√(x−1)dx (b) ∫x²eˣdx (c) ∫dx/(x²−4) (d) ∫√(4−x²)dx (e) ∫sin⁵x cos²x dx (f) ∫(x³+1)/x² dx

k5-fm-L17-P07.why:
Factor fully: x⁴ − 1 = (x−1)(x+1)(x²+1).
1/(x⁴−1) = A/(x−1) + B/(x+1) + (Cx+D)/(x²+1)
x = 1: 1 = A(2)(2) ⇒ A = 1/4
x = −1: 1 = B(−2)(2) ⇒ B = −1/4
Expanding and matching x³ coefficients: 0 = A + B + C ⇒ C = 0
Constants: 1 = A − B − D = 1/4 + 1/4 − D, so D = −1/2
= (1/4)ln|x−1| − (1/4)ln|x+1| − (1/2)arctan x + C
Factor as far as possible over the reals first. Leaving x⁴−1 as (x²−1)(x²+1) misses that x²−1 factors further.

k6-fm-L18-P01.why:
= lim(b→∞) ∫₁ᵇ x⁻³dx = lim [−1/(2x²)]₁ᵇ = lim(−1/(2b²) + 1/2) = 1/2, converges
Also immediate from the p-rule: p = 3 > 1.

k6-fm-L18-P02.why:
p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges.
Confirming: lim[2√x]₁ᵇ = lim(2√b − 2) = ∞

k6-fm-L18-P03.why:
This is Type 2: the integrand blows up at x = 0, the lower limit.
= lim(t→0⁺) ∫ₜ¹ x^(−1/2)dx = lim [2√x]ₜ¹ = lim(2 − 2√t) = 2, converges
Notice the reversal: p = 1/2 diverges on [1,∞) but converges on (0,1]. Near a spike, small p is fine; in a tail, large p is what you need.

k6-fm-L18-P04.why:
Integration by parts first: ∫xe^(−x)dx = −xe^(−x) − e^(−x) = −(x+1)e^(−x)
lim(b→∞)[−(x+1)e^(−x)]₀ᵇ = lim(−(b+1)e^(−b) + 1)
(b+1)e^(−b) → 0 since exponentials beat polynomials.
= 1, converges

k6-fm-L18-P05.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁² dx/x² or explain why it fails.
k6-fm-L18-P05.why:
The integrand blows up at x = 0, which is inside the interval, so the integral must be split.
∫₀² dx/x² = lim(t→0⁺)[−1/x]ₜ² = lim(−1/2 + 1/t) = ∞
Since one half diverges, the whole thing diverges.
Evaluating blindly gives [−1/x]₋₁² = −1/2 − 1 = −3/2, a negative answer for a positive integrand. That absurdity is the tell.

k6-fm-L18-P08.why:
First: lim(b→∞)[arctan x]₀ᵇ = π/2 − 0 = π/2
Second: split at 0. The left half gives 0 − (−π/2) = π/2. Both halves converge, so the total is π.
Both pieces must converge independently. Here they do, so the answer is legitimate, unlike ∫₋∞^∞ x dx where each half is infinite.

k6-fm-L19-P02.q: Write out S₁, S₂, S₃, S₄ for Σ(k=1) 1/2ᵏ.

k6-fm-L19-P05.why:
Sum = lim Sₙ = 3
For n ≥ 2, aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ = (3n+1)/(n+4) − (3n−2)/(n+3)
= [(3n+1)(n+3) − (3n−2)(n+4)]/((n+4)(n+3))
= [(3n²+10n+3) − (3n²+10n−8)]/((n+4)(n+3)) = 11/((n+4)(n+3))
The first term has no S₀ to subtract: a₁ = S₁ = 4/5, while the formula would give 11/20. So aₙ = 11/((n+4)(n+3)) for n ≥ 2, with a₁ = 4/5.
The relationship aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ is the bridge between the two objects, and it works in both directions.

k92-fm-L20-P03.why:
Compare growth rates: any power of ln n loses to any positive power of n.
Or apply L'Hôpital twice on (ln x)²/x: (2 ln x)/x, then 2/x → 0.
Limit is 0.

k92-fm-L20-P04.why:
Rewrite as sin(1/n)/(1/n) and let t = 1/n → 0.
lim(t→0) (sin t)/t = 1
Recognizing a Calc I limit inside a sequence is the trick here.

k7-fm-L21-P03.q: Find the sum of Σ(k=3 to ∞) 2ᵏ/5ᵏ⁻¹.
k7-fm-L21-P03.why:
Rewrite: 2ᵏ/5ᵏ⁻¹ = 5 · (2/5)ᵏ. First term at k = 3 is 5(2/5)³ = 5(8/125) = 8/25, and r = 2/5.
Sum = (8/25)/(1 − 2/5) = (8/25)/(3/5) = 8/15
Use first term over one minus ratio rather than memorizing index-shifted formulas.

k7-fm-L21-P07.q: For what values of x does Σ(k=0 to ∞) (x − 2)ᵏ/3ᵏ converge, and what is the sum?

k7-fm-L22-P03.why:
f(x) = x/(x²+1) is positive and continuous on [1,∞). Its derivative is (1 − x²)/(x²+1)² < 0 for x > 1, so it is decreasing. All three conditions hold.
∫₁^∞ x/(x²+1)dx = lim ½ln(x²+1)|₁ᵇ = ∞
The integral diverges, so the series diverges.
Note the terms do go to 0, so the Divergence Test was useless here.

k7-fm-L22-P04.why:
Integral Test with u = ln x: ∫₂^∞ dx/(x ln x) = lim ln(ln x)|₂ᵇ = ∞.
Diverges.
Contrast with Σ1/(n(ln n)²), which converges. The logarithm barely fails to save it at the first power.

k7-fm-L22-P07.why:
f(x) = 1/(x(ln x)ᵖ) is positive, continuous, decreasing on [2,∞) for p > 0.
Substitute u = ln x, du = dx/x: ∫₂^∞ dx/(x(ln x)ᵖ) = ∫ₗₙ₂^∞ du/uᵖ
That is a p-integral, converging exactly when p > 1.
So the series converges if and only if p > 1. For p ≤ 0 the terms still go to 0, so the Divergence Test settles nothing; compare instead: for n ≥ 3, ln n > 1 makes (ln n)ᵖ ≤ 1, so 1/(n(ln n)ᵖ) ≥ 1/n, and Σ1/n diverges.

k7-fm-L23-P05.why:
Bounded numerator: 2 ≤ 3 + sin n ≤ 4, so aₙ ≤ 4/n³.
Σ4/n³ converges (p = 3), so by direct comparison the series converges.
Limit comparison with bₙ = 1/n³ does not work here: the ratio aₙ/bₙ = 3 + sin n oscillates and has no limit. Direct comparison is the right tool for a bounded oscillating factor.

k8-fm-L24-P04.why:
Need aₙ₊₁ = 1/(n+1)⁴ < 0.0005 ⇒ (n+1)⁴ > 2000 ⇒ n + 1 > 6.69 ⇒ n ≥ 6.
Use 6 terms: 1 − 1/16 + 1/81 − 1/256 + 1/625 − 1/1296 ≈ 0.9468
The alternating error bound is the easiest in the course: the error is smaller than the first omitted term.

k9-fm-L28-P06.q: The Lagrange bound for the order 3 Maclaurin polynomial of sin x is |R₃(x)| ≤ |x|⁴/4!. For which x does this bound guarantee an error below 0.001?
k9-fm-L28-P06.why:
|R₃| ≤ |x|⁴/4! = |x|⁴/24 < 0.001
|x|⁴ < 0.024 ⇒ |x| < 0.024^(1/4) ≈ 0.394
So the bound guarantees the accuracy on roughly (−0.394, 0.394). Solving for the interval rather than for n is a common variant.
The true accuracy reaches further: for sine p₃ = p₄, and the R₄ bound |x|⁵/5! < 0.001 already gives |x| < 0.654. The question asks what the |x|⁴/4! bound guarantees.

k9-fm-L29-P01.q: Find the radius of convergence of Σ xᵏ/k.

k9-fm-L29-P02.q: Find the interval of convergence of Σ(k=1 to ∞) xᵏ/k.
k9-fm-L29-P02.why:
Interior: (−1, 1). Now the endpoints.
x = 1: Σ1/k, the harmonic series, diverges.
x = −1: Σ(−1)ᵏ/k, alternating harmonic, converges by the AST.
Interval: [−1, 1)
Asymmetric intervals are normal.

k9-fm-L29-P03.q: Find the interval of convergence for Σ (x + 3)ᵏ/(k² 2ᵏ).
k9-fm-L29-P03.why:
Ratio: |x+3|ᵏ⁺¹/((k+1)²2ᵏ⁺¹) · k²2ᵏ/|x+3|ᵏ = (|x+3|/2)(k/(k+1))² → |x+3|/2
Need |x+3| < 2, so R = 2 and the center is −3: interior (−5, −1).
x = −1: Σ2ᵏ/(k²2ᵏ) = Σ1/k², converges.
x = −5: Σ(−2)ᵏ/(k²2ᵏ) = Σ(−1)ᵏ/k², converges absolutely.
Interval: [−5, −1]

k9-fm-L29-P04.q: Find R for Σ k! xᵏ and for Σ xᵏ/k!.
k9-fm-L29-P04.why:
Σk!xᵏ: ratio = (k+1)|x| → ∞ unless x = 0. So R = 0, converging only at x = 0.
Σxᵏ/k!: ratio = |x|/(k+1) → 0 for every x. So R = ∞, converging everywhere.
These are the two extreme cases, and factorial placement decides which you get.

k9-fm-L29-P05.q: Find the interval of convergence for Σ (−1)ᵏ (2x − 1)ᵏ/√k.
k9-fm-L29-P05.why:
Ratio: |2x−1|√(k/(k+1)) → |2x − 1|
Need |2x − 1| < 1 ⇒ −1 < 2x − 1 < 1 ⇒ 0 < x < 1. Center 1/2, R = 1/2.
x = 1: Σ(−1)ᵏ/√k converges by the AST.
x = 0: 2x − 1 = −1, giving Σ(−1)ᵏ(−1)ᵏ/√k = Σ1/√k, a p-series with p = 1/2, diverges.
Interval: (0, 1]
When the variable has a coefficient, solve carefully for x; the radius in x is half the radius in (2x−1).

k9-fm-L29-P07.q: A power series Σcₖ(x − 2)ᵏ converges at x = 5 and diverges at x = −2. What can you say about convergence at x = 0 and x = 6?

k9-fm-L30-P01.why:
1/(1 − (−3x)) = Σ(−3x)ᵏ = Σ(−1)ᵏ3ᵏxᵏ
Converges when |3x| < 1, so R = 1/3.

k9-fm-L30-P02.why: Factor out 5 to expose the required 1: 1/(5(1 − x/5)) = (1/5)Σ(x/5)ᵏ = Σxᵏ/5ᵏ⁺¹, valid for |x| < 5.

k9-fm-L30-P04.why:
1/(1−x) = Σxᵏ. Integrating gives −ln(1−x) = Σxᵏ⁺¹/(k+1) + C.
At x = 0 both sides are 0, so C = 0.
ln(1 − x) = −Σ(k=0) xᵏ⁺¹/(k+1) = −x − x²/2 − x³/3 − …, for −1 ≤ x < 1

k9-fm-L30-P06.why:
1/(1+x⁴) = Σ(−1)ᵏx⁴ᵏ
∫₀^0.5 = Σ(−1)ᵏ(0.5)⁴ᵏ⁺¹/(4k+1) = 0.5 − 0.5⁵/5 + 0.5⁹/9 − …
= 0.5 − 0.00625 + 0.000217 − 0.0000094
≈ 0.4940
It alternates, so the error after four terms is under the fifth term, about 4×10⁻⁷.

k9-fm-L30-P07.q: Find the sum of Σ(k=1 to ∞) k/2ᵏ.
k9-fm-L30-P07.why:
Start from Σ(k=1) k xᵏ⁻¹ = 1/(1−x)². Multiply by x:
Σ(k=1) k xᵏ = x/(1−x)²
At x = 1/2: (1/2)/(1/4) = 2
Recognizing a numerical series as a known power series evaluated at a point is the standard method for summing anything with a k in the numerator.

k9-fm-L31-P01.why:
Substitute 3x into Σxᵏ/k!:
Σ(3x)ᵏ/k! = Σ3ᵏxᵏ/k!, valid for all x.

k9-fm-L31-P03.why:
e^u = Σuᵏ/k! with u = −x² gives Σ(−1)ᵏx²ᵏ/k!.
Multiply by x²: Σ(−1)ᵏx²ᵏ⁺²/k!, all x.
Substituting into a known series is always faster than differentiating this function repeatedly.

k9-fm-L31-P04.why:
sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …
Divide by x: 1 − x²/3! + x⁴/5! − … = Σ(−1)ᵏx²ᵏ/(2k+1)!
At x = 0 the series gives 1, which is the removable-singularity value and matches lim(x→0) (sin x)/x = 1.

k9-fm-L31-P05.why:
Write 1/x = 1/(1 + (x−1)) = 1/(1 − (−(x−1)))
= Σ(−(x−1))ᵏ = Σ(−1)ᵏ(x − 1)ᵏ, valid for |x − 1| < 1, that is 0 < x < 2.
Forcing the expression into the geometric form beats computing derivatives.

k9-fm-L31-P07.q: Find the Maclaurin series for f(x) = eˣ sin x through the x⁴ term.
k9-fm-L31-P07.why:
Multiply the two series and collect by degree.
eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6 + x⁴/24
sin x = x − x³/6
x¹: 1·x = x
x²: x·x = x²
x³: (x²/2)(x) + (1)(−x³/6) = x³/2 − x³/6 = x³/3
x⁴: (x³/6)(x) + (x)(−x³/6) = x⁴/6 − x⁴/6 = 0
x + x² + x³/3 + 0·x⁴ + …
Multiplying series is legal inside the common interval of convergence, and it is far easier than taking four derivatives of a product.

k10-fm-L32-P02.why: eˣ − 1 = x + x²/2 + …, so the quotient is 1 + x/2 + … → 1

k10-fm-L32-P04.q: Approximate ∫₀¹ e^(−x²) dx using the first four nonzero terms of its Maclaurin series.

k10-fm-L32-P05.why:
Odd powers with (2k+1)! and alternating signs is the sine series, with x²ᵏ⁺¹ = (π/4)²ᵏ⁺¹.
So the sum is sin(π/4) = √2/2

$hintKeys: A circle of radius 3 centered at (0, 3)

k10-fm-L34-P03.why:
Since a = 1 < b = 3, this is a limaçon with an inner loop.
It passes through the origin where r = 0: cosθ = −1/3, so θ = arccos(−1/3) ≈ 1.911 and θ ≈ 4.373 radians.
Those two angles bound the inner loop.
a: a limaçon with an inner loop
a limacon with an inner loop

k10-fm-L34-P06.q: How many intersection points do the curves r = 1 and r = 2cosθ have?

k10-fm-L34-P07.why:
The period of cos3θ is 2π/3, so as θ runs from 0 to 2π the graph is traced in six arcs, three with r > 0 and three with r < 0. A negative r plots the point in the opposite direction.
Concretely, on (π/6, π/2) we have r < 0, so those points land in the directions θ + π, between 7π/6 and 3π/2. That is exactly the petal r > 0 traces for θ in (7π/6, 3π/2). In general cos(3(θ + π)) = −cos3θ, so the point plotted at θ + π is the same point as the one at θ: the second half of the trip retraces the first. Half the arcs are duplicates, leaving 3 distinct petals.
With even n, cos(n(θ + π)) = cos nθ, so the point at θ + π is the reflection through the origin instead; the petals traced with r < 0 fall in the gaps between the others instead of on top of them, so all 2n survive.

k94-fm-L35-P04.why:
Intersect: 3sinθ = 1 + sinθ ⇒ sinθ = 1/2 ⇒ θ = π/6, 5π/6.
On that interval 3sinθ is larger (test θ = π/2: 3 vs 2).
A = ½∫_{π/6}^{5π/6} [9sin²θ − (1+sinθ)²] dθ
= ½∫ [9sin²θ − 1 − 2sinθ − sin²θ] dθ = ½∫[8sin²θ − 2sinθ − 1]dθ
8sin²θ = 4 − 4cos2θ, so the integrand is 3 − 4cos2θ − 2sinθ
= ½[3θ − 2sin2θ + 2cosθ]_{π/6}^{5π/6}
= ½[(5π/2 + √3 − √3) − (π/2 − √3 + √3)] = ½(2π) = π

k94-fm-L35-P05.why:
r = 0 when cos2θ = 0, so 2θ = ±π/2 and θ = ±π/4 bound the right loop.
A = ½∫_{−π/4}^{π/4} 4cos2θ dθ = 2[sin2θ/2]_{−π/4}^{π/4} = [sin2θ]_{−π/4}^{π/4} = 1 − (−1) = 2
Since the equation gives r² directly, no squaring step is needed.

k94-fm-L35-P07.why:
The curves meet at θ = ±π/3. Inside means taking whichever curve is smaller at each angle.
For |θ| < π/3, 2cosθ > 1, so the circle r = 1 is the inner boundary.
For π/3 < θ < π/2, 2cosθ < 1, so r = 2cosθ bounds the region.
A = 2[ ½∫₀^(π/3) 1 dθ + ½∫_{π/3}^{π/2} 4cos²θ dθ ]
= π/3 + 2∫_{π/3}^{π/2}(1 + cos2θ)dθ = π/3 + 2[θ + sin2θ/2]_{π/3}^{π/2}
= π/3 + 2[(π/2) − (π/3 + √3/4)] = π/3 + 2(π/6 − √3/4) = 2π/3 − √3/2 ≈ 1.228
Regions inside two curves nearly always require splitting at the intersection angle, because the binding curve changes.
